Q: How do HNSW and inverted-file indexes trade build cost, search effort and recall?
A: Hierarchical Navigable Small World indexes navigate a graph of vector neighborhoods; inverted-file indexes first select clusters and search their assigned vectors. Parameters trade memory, construction effort and query search breadth against approximate recall. Measure against exact search over the same eligible population and metric. Filtering and deletion can change the practical search behavior, so a benchmark without tenant constraints may not represent production. Track index generation and embedding compatibility rather than tuning parameters over a mixed representation space.
Why: An approximate index can return ten candidates before a tenant filter removes nine. Increasing requested candidates may help, but the benchmark must measure the authorized result set and final recall, not raw global nearest neighbors.
Risk: Low latency without a recall baseline can hide missing relevant results.
Trade: Use exact search for small eligible sets when approximation adds little value.
Try: Benchmark recall and latency under the actual metadata filters at several search settings.
